item.title: Neural connectomes of verbal fluency in post-stroke aphasia.
item.description:
Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society : JINS
Verbal fluency tasks are widely used to assess language abilities and executive functions in both clinical and research settings. In post-stroke patients, prior research has indicated a significant hodological contribution to the neural basis of verbal fluency; however, this has largely been examined using lesion-based measures, predefined tractography approaches, and traditional diffusion metrics. Quantitative anisotropy-based structural connectometry derived from correlational tractography was employed to determine the white matter circuits underlying semantic and phonemic fluency in 44 patients with post-stroke aphasia. Both task types were found to be linked to anterior frontal connections of left-hemisphere dorsal and ventral associative pathways, as well as domain-general projection pathways. However, visual inspection of the connectomes, supported by supplementary cross-control analyses, suggested differences in the relative emphasis and distribution of pathways, with phonemic fluency aligning more with the dorsal stream, while semantic fluency showed greater reliance on the ventral stream and a wider range of cortico-subcortical connections. The findings contribute to current understanding of the neural networks of verbal fluency in aphasia, with potential relevance for clinical practice and research.

item.title: BundleMorphometry: Spatially Resolved White Matter Bundle Shape Analysis Using Nonlinear Streamline-based Registration
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Diffusion MRI tractometry quantifies microstructural properties along white matter (WM) bundles but does not directly measure their geometry, potentially overlooking localized morphological alterations. Here, we introduce BundleMorphometry, a framework for quantifying local WM bundle shape using the analytical Jacobian of nonlinear streamline-based registration. Individual subject bundles are registered to a reference atlas bundle using BundleWarp, a streamline-based nonlinear registration method. We derive the analytical Jacobian of the resulting deformation field and compute its log-determinant (log det J) to quantify local expansion and compression at each streamline point. To enable spatially resolved group comparisons, these measurements are projected onto the two-dimensional grid, capturing variations along and across each bundle. We evaluated BundleMorphometry using two clinical datasets comprising patients with glioma and Parkinson's disease (PD). In the glioma dataset, BundleMorphometry revealed spatially extensive deformation patterns in lesion-affected WM bundles that were not captured by displacement magnitude alone. Additionally, in a group analysis of the PD dataset (32 patients and 32 healthy controls), we identified significant localized morphological differences in the corpus callosum forceps major, mid-body and right spinothalamic tract, with distinct patterns of expansion and compression. These findings demonstrate the potential of BundleMorphometry to advance conventional tractometry by enabling spatially resolved analysis of bundle morphology.

item.title: Metabolic complexity in the human brain supports metastable network dynamics and declines in normative ageing
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The adaptive capacity of the brain is tied to the complexity of its neural activity. While entropy of brain signals has been used to characterise this complexity in haemodynamic and electrophysiological systems, it remains unknown whether entropy contributes to the temporal dynamics of the metabolic signals of the brain (glucodynamics) and how metabolic entropy may relate to network organisation, brain ageing and cognitive decline. Here, we combined dynamic functional PET (fPET) with 18F-fluoroedeoxyglucose and simultaneously acquired functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in 84 adults to investigate multiscale entropy (MSE) in the brain. We report that metabolic complexity measured with PET MSE represents non-linear, high-frequency complexity, whereas hemodynamic complexity reflects non-linearly constrained neurovascular phase dynamics. Greater metabolic complexity was associated with greater network metastability, particularly in unimodal and higher-order associative networks. Greater regional metabolic complexity also correlated with greater cortical thickness, cerebral metabolic rates of glucose (CMRglc) and cerebral blood flow, and was lower in older than younger adults. In contrast, global and network haemodynamic MSE was not significant associated with network dynamics. Higher global metabolic complexity was associated with better cognitive performance, and voxel-level derived MSE clusters were \associated with cognitive performance in both modalities, with varied cluster sizes and spatial locations. However, these associations were largely accounted for by age variance. We conclude that temporal complexity in cerebral glucose is associated with the dynamics of the underlying metabolic signals, enables metastable network states and declines in ageing. Entropy of metabolic brain signals offers promise as a neurobiologically grounded metric of brain ageing.

item.title: Domestic water mineral exposure increases affective disorders vulnerability by impairing brain structural resilience
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract The neural mechanisms linking environmental mineral exposure to affective disorders remain poorly understood. Here, leveraging the large-scale UK Biobank cohort ( n = 389,984), we investigate the impact of domestic water mineral exposure on mental health. Beyond identifying population association of individual water mineral calcium (Ca) and magnesium (Mg) exposure, we developed a water mineral mixture exposure index (WMEx) to model mixture effect of Ca and Mg exposure on affective symptoms and disorders. We found that each unit increase in domestic water minerals exposure was associated with up to 0.24 standard deviation increase in elevated depressive symptoms (Ca: β = 0.24, P = 3.12 × 10 − 126 ; Mg: β = 0.07, P = 1.23×10 − 24 ; WMEx: β = 0.23, P = 1.55× 10 − 249 ), as well as an increased prospective risk of affective disorder incidence during 15.3 years follow-up (full model HR = 1.66, 95% CI: 1.40–1.96), which were all well replicated. Neuroimaging analyses uncovered the underlying neural substrates, revealing that mineral exposure was linked to impaired brain structural resilience, quantified by a novel brain structural resilience index (BSRI) representing the coupling between gray and white matter structures. Critically, causal mediation analyses demonstrated that the compromised brain structural resilience within visual-emotional circuits significantly mediated the pathway from mineral exposure to affective disorders. These neuromediating pathways were disproportionately stronger in females and individuals living in lower socioeconomic regions. Our findings reveal a crucial environmental-neurobiological axis, positioning domestic water minerals as a key determinant of mental health and highlighting how compromised brain structural resilience serves as a core neural mechanism of affective vulnerability.

item.title: Tractography-Based Insights into Neuroplasticity and Clinical Heterogeneity in Parkinson's Disease Subtypes.
item.description:
The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
Parkinson's disease shows substantial heterogeneity across motor, cognitive, and non-motor domains, reflecting variable patterns of neurodegeneration and compensation across distributed brain circuits. Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) tractography enables pathway-specific characterization of white-matter alterations and provides a framework for linking clinical subtypes to tract-level patterns that may be obscured by skeleton-based or connectomic averaging. Here, we synthesize white-matter evidence across motor, cognitive, genetic, and prodromal dimensions of PD heterogeneity, using tractography as an organizing framework within a broader dMRI and multimodal context. We review diffusion approaches ranging from diffusion tensor imaging to free-water, neurite, and fixel-based models. We distinguish pathway reconstructions from other diffusion and imaging analyses and consider how complementary approaches inform, but do not uniquely determine, interpretations of degeneration and subtype-specific neuroplasticity. Emerging methods, including harmonization pipelines, radiomic tractometry, and machine learning classifiers, may further improve tract-level sensitivity and reproducibility. Cognitive subtypes illustrate how posterior association and limbic tract degeneration, together with cholinergic and noradrenergic dysfunction, shape clinical progression. Integrating tractography with molecular, genetic, functional, and clinical markers may support subtype-specific biomarkers for risk stratification, prognosis, and targeted neuromodulation or rehabilitation strategies, although longitudinal and external validation is required before routine use.

item.title: Neural circuits, cognition, and behavior in diffuse glioma.
item.description:
Neuro-oncology
Diffuse gliomas arise within and become functionally integrated into neural circuits, establishing bidirectional interactions between malignant cells and the surrounding brain. Neuronal activity promotes glioma growth and progression, while glioma cells remodel the excitability, connectivity, and functional organization of the neural circuits they infiltrate. Pathological excitation-inhibition imbalance can impair cortical information processing, while tumor infiltration simultaneously disrupts, preserves, and induces adaptive reorganization of distributed functional networks. Language processing provides a well defined framework for examining these competing effects because language processing depends on distributed cortical and subcortical networks whose organization can be interrogated using neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and direct cortical stimulation. The pattern and severity of glioma-associated language dysfunction reflect the interaction among tumor location, growth kinetics, molecular and histopathological features, white matter involvement, and the capacity for adaptive redistribution of function within ipsilateral and contralateral networks. Slowly growing gliomas can permit substantial functional reorganization, whereas rapidly infiltrating tumors may constrain the time and biological substrate available for effective network adaptation. In this review, we examine reciprocal glioma-neural circuit interactions, with particular emphasis on the mechanisms of glioma-associated neuronal hyperexcitability and the disruption, preservation, and adaptive remodeling of language networks.

item.title: Reverberant magnetic resonance elastography and NODDI provide complementary characterisation of age-related brain changes in healthy adults.
item.description:
Physics in medicine and biology
Age-related changes in brain microstructure and mechanical properties are essential for understanding neurodegeneration and improving early diagnosis. We asked whether tissue microstructure explains the age-related decline in brain stiffness. To test this, we related stiffness measured using reverberant magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) to tissue microstructure, assessed by neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI). Approach. Twenty-eight healthy volunteers (22 to 76 years) underwent 50 Hz MRE at 3T. NODDI parameters (the isotropic volume fraction, Fiso; orientation dispersion index, ODI; neurite density index, NDI) were computed from diffusion-weighted images in 26 subjects. We analyzed global gray and white matter, as well as 13 deep brain regions. Age associations were evaluated using Spearman correlations. Multivariate regression was used to test whether NODDI parameters predicted shear modulus independently of age. All tests used Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Main results. Shear modulus decreased with age in both gray matter (ρ= -0.62, p = 0.0005) and white matter (ρ= -0.60, p = 0.0007), and in nine of 13 deep brain regions after FDR correction. Fiso (ρ = +0.55, p = 0.004) and NDI (ρ= +0.45, p = 0.023) increased with age in gray matter; no NODDI parameter changed significantly with age in white matter. Across the six global multivariate tests (gray and white matter times three NODDI parameters), only the gray-matter Fiso independently predicted shear modulus after adjusting for age (β= -3.230, pFDR = 0.010), and no NODDI parameter predicted white matter stiffness. This association did not survive FDR correction after additional adjustment for sex (pFDR = 0.073). Significance. These findings suggest that cortical free water accumulation is the microstructural measure most closely associated with age-related softening in this cohort, pending confirmation in larger, sex-balanced cohorts, and support a multi-modal approach to characterizing age-related brain changes.

item.title: Abnormalities and plasticity of white matter functional networks in opioid use disorder: a BOLD fMRI study.
item.description:
Psychological medicine
Background This study investigated the architecture and neural activity of white matter functional networks (WMFNs) in individuals with opioid use disorder (OUD) after prolonged abstinence, compared with healthy controls (HCs). Methods Blood oxygen level-dependent signals in white matter were analyzed using a data-driven k-means clustering approach across individuals with OUD at baseline (OUD1), the same individuals after prolonged abstinence at follow-up (OUD2), and HCs. Results In OUD1, the deep frontoparietal network was fragmented into the superior longitudinal fasciculus network and anterior corona radiata network; this organization partially recovered in OUD2, becoming more similar to HCs. OUD1 also showed hyperactivation in the deep frontal network and hypoactivation in the frontotemporal-parietal network, with frontotemporal-parietal activity negatively correlated with years of opioid use. Conclusions OUD is associated with disrupted architecture of WMFNs and altered neural activity, whereas prolonged abstinence may promote partial network restoration. These findings highlight the neuroplastic potential of WMFNs during recovery and provide insights into the neural mechanisms underlying OUD and abstinence-related rehabilitation.

item.title: Age-dependent structural brain aging in medication-free major depressive disorder: A multi-site analysis from COORDINATE-MDD consortium.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is associated with altered brain structure and accelerated brain aging. However, previous studies have been limited by clinical samples with mixed medication status and multiple mood states, modest sample sizes, underrepresentation of older adults with MDD, and/or reliance on summary-level data. Harmonized T1-weighted MRI from MDD (n = 645), all medication-free and in a current depressive episode, and matched healthy controls (n = 645), segmented into 145 regional volumes, from 11 sites in COORDINATE-MDD consortium. Brain age gap (BAG) was estimated cross-sectionally using gradient boosting regression with nested cross-validation. Group differences in BAG (and age-corrected BAG [cBAG]) were examined across age strata. Regional contributions were evaluated using SHAP values. MDD was associated with significantly elevated cBAG compared with healthy controls (mean difference + 2.0 years [95% CI 1.251, 2.774], Cohen's d -0.289 [95% CI -0.399, -0.179]). Age-stratified analyses showed no differences before mid-30s, with progressively larger gaps thereafter, reaching +6.8 years in MDD aged 55 and older in unadjusted analyses (4.3 years after accounting for site). cBAG differed across neuroanatomical phenotypes previously identified using COORDINATE-MDD data. Key contributing regions included lateral and medial prefrontal regions, middle temporal gyrus, putamen, supplementary motor cortex, central operculum, and cerebellum. Structural brain aging in MDD is age-dependent and most pronounced in a neuroanatomical phenotype associated with poorer key clinical outcomes. The findings are consistent with, but do not establish, neuroprogression models of MDD and demonstrate that cBAG is not a uniform feature of MDD, being more strongly expressed in a specifically clinically vulnerable disease phenotype.

item.title: DPA: Deep Parcellation Analysis for Human Trait Prediction.
item.description:
Neuroinformatics
Mapping individual differences in white matter organization is a central goal of human brain mapping. Atlas-based structural connectome analyses are widely used but are sensitive to anatomical assumptions and may miss fine-grained connectivity patterns. Data-driven fiber clustering mitigates some limitations but typically relies on streamline endpoints, overlooking rich geometric information along full trajectories. In this paper, we introduce Deep Parcellation Analysis (DPA), a geometry-aware framework for white matter parcellation and trait association. DPA samples multiscale geometric features along entire fiber streamlines and encodes them with a Multiscale Fiber AutoEncoder (MFAE) to produce compact latent representations. These enable clustering that preserves intrinsic fiber geometry independently of anatomical atlases, supporting interpretable mapping of connectivity patterns linked to individual differences. Applied to diffusion magnetic resonance imaging data from the Human Connectome Project Young Adult (HCP-YA) cohort, DPA captures white matter substrates underlying language-related cognitive traits. It achieves comparable or superior predictive performance relative to atlas-based and principal parcellation approaches while revealing biologically plausible fiber pathways. Critically, DPA identifies trait-relevant connections missed by endpoint-based methods, emphasizing the importance of full streamline geometry. Overall, DPA demonstrates that deep, geometry-informed parcellation provides a powerful, interpretable approach for linking white matter organization to behavior, advancing structure-function studies in human brain mapping.

item.title: Brain Tissue Proportionality and General Cognitive Ability Across Three Adult Cohorts
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract General cognitive ability may relate to the proportional allocation of brain tissue beyond overall tissue volume. We examined five FreeSurfer compartments using compositional data analysis: cortical gray matter, cerebral white matter, subcortical gray matter, total cerebellum, and brainstem. Human Connectome Project Young Adult data (HCP-YA; N = 1,101) provided discovery estimates; the Dallas Lifespan Brain Study (DLBS; N = 418) and Amsterdam Open MRI Collection ID1000 (AOMIC; N = 926) provided independent cohort tests. Four isometric log-ratio coordinates represented composition, with age, sex, and log total analyzed tissue volume included separately. Composition explained additional cognitive variance in DLBS (partial R² = 4.20%, p = .00154) and AOMIC (partial R² = 1.35%, p = .014). The total-cerebellum-to-cerebral-white-matter contrast selected in HCP was positive in both replication cohorts: standardized β = 0.162 (heteroskedasticity-robust 95% confidence interval 0.072–0.252) in DLBS and 0.097 (0.024–0.170) in AOMIC. Participant-pairs bootstrap intervals supported both associations. Replacing total tissue volume with estimated intracranial volume attenuated the AOMIC association, whereas including both preserved it. Relative macroanatomical allocation is associated with broad cognitive ability conditional on analyzed tissue volume, with differing effect magnitudes across cohorts. These cross-sectional findings do not establish causal tissue trade-offs.

item.title: Superior Frontal Gyrus Cortical Thickness Mediates the Association Between Openness to Experience and Theory of Mind: Evidence from the Human Connectome Project
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Background Theory of mind (ToM), the capacity to infer the mental states of others, varies considerably across healthy adults. Openness to experience has been linked both to social-cognitive abilities and to thinner prefrontal cortex, but whether cortical structure statistically accounts for the association between openness and ToM is unknown. We tested whether bilateral superior frontal gyrus (SFG) cortical thickness mediates this association. Methods Data from 1,049 healthy young adults with complete data were drawn from the Human Connectome Project. ToM was indexed by accuracy on the Heider–Simmel social animation task, openness by the NEO Five-Factor Inventory, and SFG thickness by FreeSurfer. Models adjusted for age, sex, intracranial volume and fluid intelligence; indirect effects were tested with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, and Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction was applied. Results Openness showed a positive total effect on ToM accuracy (β = .081, p = .009). Higher openness was associated with thinner left and right SFG (β = −.085 and −.084), and thinner SFG with higher ToM accuracy (β = −.082 and −.075). Indirect effects were significant (left: .0069, 95% CI [.0010, .0158]; right: .0063, 95% CI [.0007, .0146]), accounting for approximately 8.5% and 7.8% of the total effect, and remained significant after rank-based normalisation of the ceiling-affected ToM scores. Conclusions SFG cortical thickness partially and statistically mediates the association between openness to experience and social cognition. Because the data are cross-sectional and effects are small, the findings do not establish a causal mechanism, neural efficiency or synaptic pruning, but they identify a candidate structural pathway for longitudinal testing.

item.title: Adaptive and maladaptive microstructural remodelling of the maternal brain revealed by diffusion kurtosis imaging
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Postpartum depression (PPD) is a major maternal mental health concern that may arise during neurobiological and emotional adaptation. Alterations in these adaptive processes may contribute to depressive symptom vulnerability; however, the neurobiological basis of postpartum brain adaptation remains unclear. We investigated microstructural brain remodelling in postpartum women using diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI) and evaluated its association with Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) scores. We compared brain magnetic resonance imaging findings between 15 women one month postpartum and 10 nulliparous women without psychiatric disorders. Tract-based spatial statistics and regions of interest were analysed using diffusion tensor and kurtosis metrics. Compared with nulliparous women, postpartum women showed significantly lower mean and axial diffusivity values in white matter regions, including the frontal lobe, basal ganglia, and corticospinal tract. The posterior insular cortex showed increased mean and radial kurtosis, whereas the putamen demonstrated decreased diffusivity. EPDS scores showed positive correlations with kurtosis metrics in the amygdala and negative correlations with diffusivity metrics in the hypothalamus. These findings suggest that the postpartum brain undergoes coordinated microstructural remodelling involving emotional regulation, stress response, and maternal behavioural adaptations. Thus, DKI may provide an objective neuroimaging biomarker for identifying maladaptive postpartum brain changes associated with depressive symptoms.

item.title: Posterior cortical gray matter heterogeneity between hyposmia- and RBD-defined prodromal phenotypes in Parkinson's disease: a PPMI voxel-based morphometry study
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Prodromal Parkinson's disease (PD) includes clinically distinct enrollment phenotypes. We examined whole-brain gray matter volume (GMV) in Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) participants recruited through hyposmia-only or REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD)-only pathways and assessed the stability of the findings. Methods Baseline T1-weighted MRI from 465 hyposmia-only and 149 RBD-only participants (N = 614) was analyzed with CAT12/SPM25 voxel-based morphometry (VBM). Models included age, sex, intracranial volume, and scanner family. Whole-brain clusters were defined at voxel p < 0.001 and tested using family-wise error (FWE) correction. We examined scanner-restricted samples, 123 sex/scanner-matched pairs, and 10,000-sign-flip permutation analysis of linear models (PALM). Bilateral cuneus/calcarine estimates and clinical assessments were exploratory. Results Whole-brain analysis identified a posterior phenotype effect (F cluster: k = 4,499; pFWE = 4.15×10⁻⁷), with higher GMV in hyposmia-only participants. In 123 matched pairs, a posterior H > RBD T cluster survived correction (pFWE = 0.0266), whereas the F contrast did not. PALM also identified a posterior effect (two-sided threshold-free cluster enhancement [TFCE] FWE p = 0.0027; voxelwise FWE p = 0.0277). Adjusted bilateral cuneus differences were + 0.211 mL (95% CI 0.095–0.327) in the full cohort and + 0.187 mL (0.041–0.333) after matching. MRI-proximal RBD screening questionnaire scores showed no significant association with regional GMV. Conclusions Posterior cortical GMV differed between these enrollment-defined prodromal phenotypes. The anatomical finding was supported by nonparametric inference, although the matched F test and strictest scanner restriction were nonsignificant. Longitudinal studies are needed to establish its clinical relevance.

item.title: Longitudinal Changes in the Cortico-Reticulospinal Tract Associated with High-Intensity Locomotor Training in Chronic Stroke.
item.description:
Neurorehabilitation and neural repair
Introduction High-intensity locomotor training (HIT) is recommended for improving walking capacity, but treatment responses are variable. Understanding the brain changes underlying responsiveness to training could provide insight into this variability. Emerging evidence suggests upregulation of the contralesional cortico-reticulospinal tract (CRST) may contribute to walking function after stroke. However, it is unclear whether CRST upregulation is supportive or maladaptive, and no studies have examined CRST changes after HIT. This study investigated how CRST and corticospinal tract (CST) strength and laterality reorganize, and their relationship with walking capacity after locomotor HIT. Methods Ten participants with chronic stroke completed a 4-week no-intervention control phase then 4 weeks of HIT. Diffusion MRI and 6-minute walk distance were obtained at weeks 0, 4, and 8. Analysis tested changes in ipsilesional and contralesional CRST and CST strength and laterality. Associations between changes in tract laterality and walking capacity were examined. Results During the treatment phase (vs the control phase), there were significantly greater increases in contralesional CRST strength (1.02 SD [95% CI: 0.25, 1.79]), contralesional CRST laterality (4.44 [2.15, 6.72]), and 6-minute walk distance (33 meters [17, 50]). Walking capacity improvements were associated with changes in CRST laterality (r = 0.77, P = .01), but not CST laterality (r = -0.01, P = 0.98). Discussion Following HIT, increases in contralesional CRST strength and laterality were observed. CRST laterality changes were strongly associated with walking improvements, suggesting an association between contralesional CRST changes and training-related improvements. item.title: Six-Month Music Practice Versus Psychomotor Interventions in Mild Cognitive Impairment: Behavioral and Hippocampal Outcomes.
item.description:
Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is characterized by measurable cognitive decline with largely preserved daily functioning and increased risk of dementia. MCI patients may also exhibit sensorimotor and communication impairments, while hippocampal atrophy and altered functional connectivity are prominent neural features associated with further cognitive decline. Evidence from nonpharmacological interventions integrating cognitive challenge, coordinated movement, and emotional engagement remains limited in early-stage MCI. In this pilot intervention study, we examined whether 6 months of intensive musical instrument training versus psychomotor interventions were associated with changes in cognitive and sensorimotor performance, hippocampal gray matter volume, and functional connectivity. Outcomes were compared between randomized MCI groups, with matched healthy controls as reference for test-retest and age-related neural effects. Improvements in global cognition were modest, reaching marginal significance only in the music group, while both interventions were associated with complementary domain-specific cognitive and sensorimotor gains. Hippocampal gray matter volume remained stable across all three groups, whereas hippocampal functional connectivity declined in healthy controls but remained stable in both intervention groups, consistent with possible functional neural maintenance. These preliminary findings suggest that group-based, low-risk music and psychomotor interventions may support cognitive, sensorimotor, and neural functioning in early MCI, warranting further investigation in larger controlled trials.

item.title: Multidimensional MRI Reveals Cellular-Scale Microstructural Phenotypes in Human Brain Aging.
item.description:
Aging cell
Brain aging is accompanied by profound cellular and microstructural changes that precede overt tissue loss, yet in vivo MRI studies largely emphasize macroscopic measures or isolated diffusion and relaxation metrics, providing limited insight into how cellular-scale tissue architecture is altered across the adult lifespan. Here, we apply multidimensional diffusion-relaxation MRI (MD-MRI) to map voxel-wise microstructural phenotypes in cognitively unimpaired adults spanning early adulthood to late life (23-77 years). Rather than relying on predefined compartment models, MD-MRI resolves continuous voxel-wise distributions in a joint diffusion-relaxation space, enabling an integrated, model-free description of how cellular shape, size, restriction, and chemical environment vary with age. Using this approach, we reveal age-related multilateral shifts within a complex microstructural landscape, marked by increasing heterogeneity and disorder across brain tissue. With age, cellular-scale features showed a systematic transition from small to larger length-scale structures accompanied by reduced microscopic restriction, indicating a loss of fine cellular barriers and expansion of extracellular space. In parallel, we show tissue-dependent alterations in fast-relaxing properties aligned with known gray- and white-matter aging processes, including iron accumulation and myelin loss. Together, these findings indicate that normative brain aging involves progressive reorganization of structure and composition at the cellular level, rather than uniform shifts in bulk tissue properties. By decoupling cellular-scale shape, size, restriction, and chemical environment in vivo, MD-MRI identifies increasing cellular heterogeneity and breakdown of microscopic restriction as central features of human brain aging and provides a biologically interpretable framework for linking microstructural reorganization to age-related functional decline.

item.title: Serum brain-derived tau in lacunar stroke and cerebral small vessel disease.
item.description:
European stroke journal
Introduction Brain-derived tau (BD-tau) selectively quantifies tau of central nervous system origin in blood and has demonstrated strong correlations with infarct volume and functional outcome in general ischaemic stroke, but data in lacunar stroke and cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) are lacking. Patients and methods In a prospectively collected cohort of 101 lacunar stroke patients with an MRI-confirmed recent small subcortical infarct (RSSI) and 47 controls, we measured serum BD-tau using the HD-X SIMOA platform at baseline and 3 and 15 months after stroke. We examined associations of BD-tau with infarct size, chronic CSVD neuroimaging features (white matter hyperintensities [WMHs], lacunes, microbleeds, total SVD score), CSVD progression on follow-up MRI and functional outcome. Results Baseline serum BD-tau was higher in RSSI patients than controls (median 9.54 [7.32-12.20] vs 7.75 [6.18-9.44] pg/mL; P = .003) and correlated with infarct diameter (rs = 0.222, P = 0.039). Brain-derived tau did not correlate with time from stroke symptom onset to blood sampling (rs = 0.150, P = .179). Brain-derived tau was not associated with chronic CSVD neuroimaging features (WMHs, lacunes, microbleeds, SVD score; all P > .05) at any timepoint. Longitudinally, BD-tau returned to control levels by 3 months (P = .374) and remained stable at 15 months (P = .985). Brain-derived tau was neither associated with new vascular MRI lesions on follow-up nor functional neurological outcome. Conclusion Serum BD-tau is elevated acutely in CSVD-related RSSI, correlates with infarct size and normalises by 3 months. Brain-derived tau was not associated with chronic CSVD neuroimaging features or disease progression, suggesting sensitivity to acute neuronal injury rather than chronic or progressive CSVD.

item.title: Diagnostic and sex effects on frontostriatal brain wiring structural organization in early psychosis affective subjects compared to healthy controls.
item.description:
Molecular psychiatry
Background Brain connectivity abnormalities may underlie affective psychosis which may be influenced by sex. Using diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) tractography, we assessed frontostriatal brain wiring connectivity patterns in 46 early psychosis affective and 56 healthy control young adult, male and female participants. Methods We collected harmonized whole brain tractography dMRI data from three sites and applied our novel fiber clustering methodology to identify 17 white matter fiber clusters connecting the frontal cortex and caudate per hemisphere in each group. By comparing cortical and caudate inter-cluster endpoint distances between groups, we assessed their patterns of frontostriatal connectivity. Results 1) In both males and females in early affective psychosis and healthy controls, bilaterally, the frontal cortex to caudate wiring pattern deviated from a topographic organization. 2) in a right hemisphere frontal pole fiber cluster, independent of sex, we found a significant interaction effect of diagnosis on the connectivity pattern between frontal cortex and caudate, (p = 0.013); 3) in a left hemisphere inferior frontal gyrus, pars triangularis, fiber cluster, we found sex influenced the significant interaction effect of diagnosis on the connectivity pattern between frontal cortex and caudate, (p = 0.0085), with the effect much greater in females (p < 0.00001) than in males (p = 0.97); and, 4) post-hoc tests showed a significant effect of diagnosis on the pattern of frontal cortex to caudate connectivity in specific subregions (ps ≤0.04). Conclusions Importantly, while the frontostriatal wiring pattern in both early affective psychosis and healthy controls deviated from a topographic organization, we found in a right hemisphere fiber cluster, independent of sex, that a significant interaction effect of diagnosis was observed on the frontal cortex to caudate connectivity pattern, whereas, in a left hemisphere fiber cluster, the effect of diagnosis on connectivity pattern was influenced by sex, showing the importance of the role of sex in brain wiring patterns in early affective psychosis.

item.title: Hippocampal Subfield Volumes and Spatial Memory Performance in Older Adults At-Risk for Type 2 Diabetes.
item.description:
Hippocampus
Older adults at risk for type 2 diabetes (T2D) are more likely to experience accelerated cognitive aging and neurodegeneration due to impaired metabolism in the hippocampus. However, the precise relationship between T2D risk factors, brain volumes (i.e., gray matter, white matter, hippocampus subfields), and hippocampus-dependent functions (i.e., spatial pattern separation, a component of spatial memory) remains unexplored. To investigate these relationships in this cross-sectional study, 60 older adults at risk for T2D (e.g., high BMI or elevated A1c levels) completed a touchscreen-based spatial pattern separation behavioral task-the Trial-Unique delayed Nonmatching-to-Location (TUNL) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). HippUnfold was utilized to segment the hippocampus from high-resolution, T1 -weighted images. We found positive correlations between A1c levels and volumes of the dentate gyrus (DG) and cornu ammonis (CA) 2, indicating that higher A1c was associated with larger volumes of hippocampal subregions. Additionally, TUNL accuracy was correlated with gray matter and distinct hippocampus subfield volumes (i.e., subiculum, CA1, and CA4), with larger volumes associated with better spatial memory performance. Understanding early structural changes in T2D risk allows us to further characterize changes in brain health associated with metabolic dysfunction.

item.title: Fixel-wise differences in White Matter Fiber-bundle Cross-section identified in Children who Stutter
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Developmental stuttering has been repeatedly linked to decreased white matter integrity and structural connectivity differences in major white matter tracts. Prior diffusion-weighted MRI studies reporting such white matter structural differences involved voxel-averaged tensor measures (e.g., fractional anisotropy (FA)). A well-acknowledged limitation of this approach, however, has been that it cannot resolve distinct fiber populations within crossing-fiber regions. Fixel-based analysis addresses this limitation by quantifying individual fiber populations within a voxel and providing complementary measures of fiber density (FD), fiber-bundle cross-section (FC), and their combined measure (FDC). Here we applied Fixel-based analysis to diffusion MRI data from 171 children aged 3–13 years, including 84 children who stutter and 87 typically developing controls, to test whether white-matter differences associated with developmental stuttering were expressed as differences in FD, FC, and FDC and whether these measures show group-specific age-related patterns. We evaluated this at both the whole-brain level and within a priori white-matter tracts. FC, but not FD or FDC, showed significant Group and Group × Age effects, indicating that white-matter differences were primarily expressed in fiber-bundle macrostructure. Tract-of-interest analyses identified developmental differences in bilateral arcuate fasciculus FC that remained significant across tracts, with controls showing greater age-related increases in FC than children who stutter. Additional FC differences were observed across corticospinal and thalamocortical pathways, although these tract-wise effects were less robust to across-tract correction. These findings suggest that white-matter differences in developmental stuttering are prominently expressed in fiber-bundle macrostructure rather than fiber density and highlight divergent development of bilateral arcuate pathways. FBA provides fiber-specific information that complements conventional tensor-based diffusion measures and may improve characterization of white-matter development in childhood stuttering. Significance Statement Developmental stuttering has repeatedly been associated with white-matter differences, but conventional diffusion measures cannot readily distinguish changes in individual fiber populations within regions containing crossing fibers. Using Fixel-based analysis in children who stutter, we show that these differences are primarily expressed in fiber-bundle cross-section rather than fiber density, implicating macrostructural differences in white-matter organization. The strongest tract-wise developmental effects were observed bilaterally in the arcuate fasciculus, a major pathway supporting auditory-motor integration, where children who stutter showed divergent age-related trajectories relative to typically developing children. These findings provide a fiber-specific perspective on the neurodevelopmental basis of stuttering and refine the interpretation of white-matter differences previously identified using conventional diffusion imaging.

item.title: Occupational Exposure Rather Than Trauma: Lower Occipital Gray Matter Volume in Underground Coal Miners Without PTSD or Other Psychiatric Diagnoses.
item.description:
Neurotoxicology
Underground coal mining involves extreme conditions such as inadequate lighting, chronic exposure to dust and toxic gases, and intense occupational stress. Cortical changes observed in miners have been addressed almost exclusively in the literature within the framework of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), neglecting the possibility that these changes may stem directly from environmental exposure independently of psychopathology. The potential for work-specific conditions such as prolonged dark work, insufficient daylight, and exposure to toxic dust to lead to structural brain changes even without any psychopathology has been overlooked. To address this gap, 28 underground miners and 28 surface miners, who were free of current psychiatric and neurological diagnoses, were compared. T1 images obtained from 3T MRI were analyzed using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) with CAT12/SPM12. Relationships between gray matter volume, working time, and neuropsychological performance were examined using a generalized additive model (GAM). Significantly lower gray matter volume was detected in the left occipital cortex (calcarine fissure, lingual and inferior occipital gyrus) of miners (t(53) = 4.82, pFWE = 0.026, d = 1.32). The effect was regionally selective. Occipital volume was negatively correlated with underground work time (r = -0.422), while this correlation was absent in the control group (r = 0.013). GAM showed significant nonlinear relationships between morphometry and learning score, recall and TMT-B (R² = 89%). This study is one of the first to associate occipital volume reduction in miners with chronic occupational exposure independently of psychological trauma. The findings are critically important for occupational health policies targeting neurological protection.

item.title: Distinct gradients of cortical architecture capture visual representations and behavior across the lifespan.
item.description:
eLife
The microstructure of cells within the human cerebral cortex varies across the cortical ribbon, where changes in cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture are thought to endow each region of the cortex with its unique function. While fine-scale relative to a cell, these changes at the population level impact architectural properties of the cortex measurable in vivo by noninvasive MRI, such as the thickness and myelin content of the cortex. This raises the question of whether or not we can use these in vivo architectural measures to understand cortical organization, function, and development more broadly. Using the human visual cortex as a test bed, we demonstrated two architectural gradients, one in which cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture converge and another in which they diverge. These two gradients underlie the structural and functional topography of the visual cortex, even predicting the presence of new visual representations. Moreover, the two gradients show distinct visual behavior relevance and lifespan trajectory. These findings provide a more general framework for understanding the human cortex, showing that architectural gradients are a measurable fingerprint of functional organization and ontogenetic routines in the human brain.

item.title: NeuroPack: Advanced Learnable Packaging Toolkit Towards Ultra-High Compression Ratio for Volumetric Neuroimaging
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
High-throughput 3D microscopic imaging generates brain-volume datasets at terabyte to petabyte scale, posing significant storage challenges for large-scale neuroimaging data. In this study, we introduce NeuroPack , a hyperprior-driven 3D deep-learning-based packaging toolkit specifically designed for compressing 3D microscopic volumes at the mesoscale. NeuroPack encodes a compact hyperprior stream that conditions its entropy model on local voxel-wise variance, adaptively allocating bits to preserve mesoscale anatomical details for an optimal rate-distortion balance. To ensure reproducible deployment across heterogeneous microscopy datasets and computing environments, NeuroPack implements model integerization for the hyperprior side-information pathway, whose hyper-decoder predicts the Gaussian mean and scale parameters used by the arithmetic coder. By replacing platform-dependent floating-point hyper-decoding with deterministic fixed-point integer convolutions, NeuroPack produces bit-exact entropy models across CPUs, GPUs, local workstations, and cloud servers, thereby preventing decoding drift caused by floating-point rounding, fused-multiply-add ordering, or library-specific kernels. This integerized design preserves rate-distortion behavior while maintaining efficient encoding and decoding for large anisotropic 3D microscopy volumes. Our method enables high-fidelity microscopy reconstruction at 100- to 1000-fold compression across diverse modalities and species. Quantitatively, NeuroPack delivers the strongest overall rate-distortion performance in both BD-PSNR and BD-MSSSIM, with average relative gains of 73.4% and 50.8%, respectively, over the best competing codec. Importantly, NeuroPack preserves image fidelity required for downstream morphological reconstruction and analysis, as validated by simultaneous human annotation of original and decompressed confocal whole-brain zebrafish microscopy images. Together, NeuroPack provides a learning-based compression framework explicitly tailored for microscopy data, establishing a scalable storage solution for data-intensive neuroimaging and AI-empowered biological discovery.

item.title: Salience network expansion as a transdiagnostic neural marker for psychopathology risk in adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Increased cortical surface area of the brain’s salience network (SAL) has been observed in depression and appears to emerge during early adolescence. However, similar expansion has also been reported in bipolar disorder (BD), obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), and other atypicalities of salience network function have been broadly implicated across multiple psychiatric conditions. Whether increased SAL surface area is specific to depression or related more generally with psychopathology remains unclear. Using data collected as part of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (baseline: N = 7942; ages 9–10; Year 2: N = 5901; ages 11–12), we quantified individual SAL size and examined associations with dimensional symptoms from the Child Behavior Checklist. SAL surface area showed substantial inter-individual variability, with expansion occurring primarily through encroachment into the default mode (DMN), action-mode (AMN), and frontoparietal (FP) networks. Larger SAL size showed a modest positive association with depressive symptoms in the baseline sample, consistent with prior reports; however, this association did not replicate in the year 2 internal replication sample. Instead, associations with total problems were stronger and replicated across both timepoints, suggesting a subtle, dimensional relationship between SAL organization and general psychopathology burden. These findings suggest that individual differences in SAL organization may represent a broader transdiagnostic neural correlate of dimensional psychopathology rather than a disorder-specific neural signature.

item.title: Algorithmic Geometry Shapes the Biological Meaning of Thalamocortical Structural Covariance
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Neuroimaging studies often derive and discuss structural covariance (SC) as a representation of underlying brain circuitry that reflects coordinated maturation, anatomical connectivity, transcriptional similarity, and shared genetic influences. These associations motivate its use to study brain organization across development, aging, and disease. However, the algorithms used to derive SC networks impose constraints that may shape their biological interpretation. To understand the impact of algorithm choice, we used the thalamocortical system as an example and compared five common representations of voxelwise SC, namely, principal component analysis (PCA), independent component analysis (ICA), non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), orthogonal projective NMF (OPNMF), and k -means clustering, in 755 participants aged 8–22 years from the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort (PNC). SC networks derived from deformation-based morphometry (DBM) were evaluated against three complementary biological benchmarks: age-related individual differences, fractional-anisotropy (FA)-based microstructural connectivity of regionally-specific thalamocortical connections, and Allen Human Brain Atlas gene expression. Each algorithm demonstrated underlying sensitivity to differing aspects of neurobiology: PCA and OPNMF showed the strongest associations between participant-level component weights and age. NMF, OPNMF, and k -means showed greater spatial overlap between positive cortical SC and tractography-derived projections. ICA and PCA showed stronger correspondence between thalamic and cortical gene-expression profiles across the transcriptome, whereas NMF, OPNMF, and k -means more often identified thalamic components with relatively high core-matrix gene expression. This study emphasizes that algorithmic constraints effectively act as biological priors and decomposition methods do not provide neutral compression of the data. We conclude that it is critical to consider whether the algorithmic objective matches the representational geometry of the neurobiology being studied. Overall, our findings suggest that SC studies should select and justify algorithms according to the biological question, explicitly considering whether their constraints favour distributed gradients, overlapping regional parts, or discrete clusters. Meanwhile, interpretations of SC findings could also be informed by the specific algorithmic constraints used to derive them.

item.title: Constantin von Economo (1876-1931): cytoarchitectonic roots of modern network neuroscience.
item.description:
Journal of neurosurgery
Constantin von Economo (1876-1931) is widely remembered for his seminal description of encephalitis lethargica, yet his broader contribution to cortical organization remains underappreciated. Beyond clinical neurology, von Economo and Georg Koskinas, a neurologist-psychiatrist, contributed to the broader cytoarchitectonic tradition by developing one of the most detailed architectonic frameworks of the human cerebral cortex, emphasizing laminar heterogeneity, regional transition, and structural specialization. These concepts can be reconsidered in relation to contemporary models of large-scale brain organization. In particular, cortical territories associated with von Economo's work, including the anterior insula and anterior cingulate region, are now recognized as key hubs in salience processing and contain the distinctive spindle-shaped neurons later termed von Economo neurons. Recent advances in connectomics, cortical gradient mapping, and laminar neuroimaging have renewed interest in the relationship between cortical microstructure and distributed functional networks. From this perspective, von Economo's work may be viewed not simply as a landmark in classical neuroanatomy, but as a historically important structural framework that can be reinterpreted in relation to modern ideas of structure-function coupling and network-level brain organization. This historical vignette revisits his life, scientific contributions, and enduring relevance to contemporary neuroscience and neurosurgical thinking.

item.title: Neural and cognitive correlates of adolescent anxiety: Widespread brain network alterations, increased control costs, and visuospatial processing deficits.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
This study investigated the neural substrates and cognitive correlates of adolescent anxiety, which are currently incompletely understood, in N = 3,499 youth with median (IQR) age 12.0 (1.1) years (~51.0% females), from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Study. Resting-state fMRI, structural MRI, anxiety (scores and related disorder diagnoses), and neurocognitive data were analyzed. Mixed-effects regression models were used to examine associations between anxiety, brain characteristics (topological and morphometric properties, and regulatory (control) costs of intrinsic network dynamics), and cognitive outcomes. Females, older youth, and those with more parental mental health problems had higher anxiety (β = 0.04-1.15, 95% CI = [0.01, 2.18]). Higher resting-state connectivity and/or centrality (network importance) of the cerebellum, amygdala, and thalamus, and higher cerebellum-basal-ganglia-thalamus control costs were associated with higher anxiety (β = 0.04-0.08, 95% CI = [0.01, 0.11]). In contrast, temporoparietal and frontoparietal network efficiency and resilience (robustness) were protective for social and/or generalized anxiety disorders (adjusted odds ratio (aOR) = 0.72-0.80, 95% CI = [0.62, 0.98]). Higher cortical thickness and/or volume of the superior temporal gyrus, pars opercularis, precentral gyrus, and putamen were associated with higher odds of generalized or social anxiety disorder (aOR = 1.28-1.44, 95% CI = [1.07, 1.78]). Finally, anxiety was associated with lower response accuracy in the Little Man Task (β = -0.05, 95% CI = [-0.09, -0.01]), and attenuated positive brain-task performance associations. These findings suggest that adolescent anxiety is associated with widespread brain alterations, especially in the cerebellum-basal ganglia-thalamus network, while the organization of frontoparietal and temporoparietal networks, which play as key role in emotion regulation and social function, is protective for anxiety disorders. It is also associated with lower visuospatial processing and alterations in the networks that support it.

item.title: A case study of early-emerging prosopometamorphopsia.
item.description:
Cognitive neuropsychology
Prosopometamorphopsia (PMO) is a rare perceptual disorder characterized by facial distortions. This report presents the first thorough study of early-emerging PMO. Zed, who was 15 years old when first tested, has experienced lifelong, dynamic facial distortions in which features move, droop, disappear, expand, and rotate. He also experiences identity misrecognitions, perceiving familiar faces as strangers and vice versa. Behavioural assessments indicate Zed's distortions persist across different viewpoints, visual field positions, picture-plane orientations, and visual angles. Neuropsychological testing revealed deficits in face identity recognition, yet Zed performed normally on tests requiring fine-grained perception of facial age and sex. While structural MRI showed no lesions, MRI revealed reduced face-selectivity in right posterior face-selective areas, and diffusion tensor imaging indicated lower white matter integrity in the left inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus. This case offers novel insights into the manifestations of early-emerging PMO, its co-occurrence with other face-processing disorders, and its underlying neural correlates.

item.title: Association of neighborhood opportunity and abdominal obesity with brain development and cognitive function in adolescents: A prospective cohort analysis.
item.description:
Annals of epidemiology
Objective To investigate the longitudinal associations between neighborhood opportunity and brain structure and cognitive performance among adolescents, and to explore whether these associations differ by sex, maturational status, race/ethnicity, and abdominal obesity trajectory. Methods Prospective data from ABCD Study participants with complete baseline data (n = 9375; ages 9-10 years, 47% girls; 21 U.S. sites), followed from 2016 to 2018-2020-2022, were analyzed; outcome-specific analytic samples were 9121 at 2 years and 3048 at 4 years. Neighborhood opportunity was measured with the Childhood Opportunity Index (COI) 2.0, subcortical volumes with MRI, and cognition with the NIH Toolbox. Mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline outcome, age, sex, race/ethnicity, population density, and time-varying waist-to-height ratio; sex differences were tested directly. Results Mean (SD) baseline age was 9.9 (0.6) years, and 54.4% were White. Very-high versus very-low COI was associated with larger subcortical volumes (e.g., amygdala 25.33 mm³; 95% CI 11.98-38.69, at 2 years) and higher memory scores at 2 years (5.56 points; 4.55-6.57) and 4 years (6.68; 4.44-8.91). Associations with the amygdala (2 years) and caudate (both waves) were larger in girls than in boys; cognitive associations did not differ by sex. Four-year estimates were similar to or larger than 2-year estimates; loss of statistical significance reflected the smaller 4-year samples. Conclusions Adolescents from socioeconomically disadvantaged environments experience significant disparities in brain structure and cognitive function, which exploratory stratified analyses suggesting variation by abdominal obesity and sociodemographic characteristics including sex, maturational status, and race/ethnicity.

item.title: The impact of pruning iterations on Arcuate Fasciculus morphometry and diffusion features in right-handed adults.
item.description:
Radiological physics and technology
To evaluate the utility of a pruning method in refining tractography and to examine the Arcuate Fasciculus (AF) morphometry and diffusion metrics in right-handed adults. Thirty-two healthy, right-handed adults underwent DTI on a 1.5T MRI system. Q-space diffeomorphic reconstruction was performed on a single-shell DTI dataset, and the AF was automatically tracked. Topology-Informed Pruning (TIP) was applied to reduce false-positive streamlines across varying numbers of iterations. Morphometry and diffusion metrics of the bilateral AF were extracted. The associations between these metrics and the number of iterations were evaluated using correlation analysis. The protocol-specific TIP threshold was identified as the knee point using the Kneedle algorithm. Differences in the morphometry and diffusion metrics of the selection AF tractometry by sex and hemisphere were also examined. A pFDR < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. TIP-based pruning was associated with improved tract delineation through the reduction of spurious streamlines. The number of pruning iterations affected the AF's morphometry and diffusion metrics. The selected TIP threshold was 8, and TIPs greater than 8 yielded stable values with minimal variability. Significant differences between hemispheres were observed in diffusion metrics except quantitative anisotropy (QA). For morphometry metrics, significant differences were identified in the number of tracts, span, and curl (pFDR < 0.05). No significant sex-related differences were found after FDR correction. Pruning iterations affect the visualization of AF in the protocol-specific population of right-handed adults. The number of pruning iterations selected should be carefully determined with full awareness and consideration.

item.title: Brain and Cardiometabolic Effects of Major Weight Loss in People With Obesity: Preliminary Cohort Findings.
item.description:
Obesity science & practice
Objective Given the overlap between obesity-related metabolic and vascular abnormalities and Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk factors, it is critical to determine whether weight loss improves brain and cardiovascular health. This study examined whether ≥ 40% excess-weight loss is associated with improvements in cardiometabolic risk, brain structure, and cognition. Methods The study was a longitudinal study of individuals with obesity undergoing metabolic and bariatric surgery or medical/behavioral weight-loss treatment. Participants were classified at follow-up as weight-loss (WL; ≥ 40% excess-weight loss) or non-weight-loss (nWL; < 40%). All completed medical evaluations, structural MRI, and cognitive testing at baseline and 1 year. Results At 1 year, the WL group exhibited improvements in BMI, HbA1C, inflammatory, metabolic, and lipid profiles. MRI-based volumetrics revealed increases in subcortical gray-matter volume and preservation of AD-vulnerable regions. Cognitive performance remained unchanged. Conclusions Achieving ≥ 40% excess-weight loss was associated with improvements in metabolic health and brain structure, including favorable subcortical volume increases. These findings underscore the potential of sustained weight reduction to mitigate risks linked to metabolic syndromes and neurodegeneration. Longer-term follow-up is warranted to determine whether continued metabolic improvements lead to detectable cognitive gains and additional brain-health benefits beyond 1 year.
